lesson.text: Hmph. Another climber. I'm Newman. I've been stuck on this ledge so long I can only see molecules END-ON. Don't ask. Let's get this over with.
Alkanes are the simplest family: only carbon and hydrogen, and only single bonds. Chemists call them SATURATED hydrocarbons, because every carbon holds as many hydrogens as it possibly can.
That gives every alkane the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Count the carbons, double it, add two. Five carbons? C₅H₁₂. Even a gargoyle can do that.
Memorize the first ten names. I'm not repeating them. Meth-, eth-, prop-, but- (1 to 4), then the Greek counting: pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-, non-, dec- (5 to 10). Add -ane.
lesson.art: 1 meth · 2 eth · 3 prop · 4 but · 5 pent · 6 hex · 7 hept · 8 oct · 9 non · 10 dec

lesson.text: Four carbons can line up in a row (butane) or branch (isobutane, 2-methylpropane). Same formula, C₄H₁₀, different connections. Those are CONSTITUTIONAL ISOMERS: different compounds with different properties.
Worked example: what's the formula of octane? Eight carbons: 2 × 8 + 2 = 18 hydrogens. C₈H₁₈. There. Now go away and answer some questions.

problems.prompt: What's the molecular formula of heptane?
problems.hint: Hept- means 7. Use CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

explain.f-c7h16: Right! Hept- is 7 carbons, and 2 × 7 + 2 = 16. Heptane is C₇H₁₆.
explain.f-c7h14: C₇H₁₄ is two hydrogens short. That's CₙH₂ₙ, which means a ring or a double bond. An alkane is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: C₇H₁₆.
explain.f-c7h12: C₇H₁₂ is four hydrogens short of an alkane. Heptane is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: C₇H₁₆.
explain.f-c6h14: C₆H₁₄ is hexane, with 6 carbons. Hept- means 7: C₇H₁₆.

problems.prompt: A straight-chain alkane has the formula C₉H₂₀. What is it called?
problems.hint: Count the carbons, then use the Greek prefix.

explain.nm-nonane: Right! Nine carbons: non- plus -ane. Nonane, C₉H₂₀.
explain.nm-octane: Octane has 8 carbons (C₈H₁₈). Nine carbons is nonane.
explain.nm-decane: Decane has 10 carbons (C₁₀H₂₂). Nine is nonane.
explain.nm-heptane: Heptane has 7 carbons (C₇H₁₆). Nine is nonane.

problems.prompt: Why are alkanes called SATURATED hydrocarbons?
problems.hint: Saturated with what?

explain.sat-maxh: Right! With only C–C and C–H single bonds, each carbon holds the maximum possible number of hydrogens. They're 'saturated' with hydrogen.
explain.sat-water: Alkanes barely dissolve in water at all. 'Saturated' means each carbon holds the most hydrogens possible, because all bonds are single.
explain.sat-ring: Rings aren't required (butane has none). 'Saturated' means only single bonds, so the maximum number of hydrogens per carbon.
explain.sat-double: Backwards! Double bonds make a compound UNsaturated. Alkanes have only single bonds, so they hold the most hydrogens possible.

problems.prompt: Butane and isobutane (2-methylpropane) are both C₄H₁₀. What are they to each other?
problems.hint: Same formula. Are the atoms connected the same way?

explain.iso-const: Right! Same formula, different connections (four in a row vs. branched). They're constitutional isomers: different compounds with different boiling points.
explain.iso-same: No rotation or redrawing turns butane into isobutane. The atoms are connected differently, so they're different compounds: constitutional isomers.
explain.iso-conf: Conformers differ only by rotation around single bonds. Butane and isobutane have different connections, so they're constitutional isomers.
explain.iso-diff: Both are C₄H₁₀, so they ARE isomers. Different connections make them constitutional isomers.

problems.prompt: Match each drawing to its name.
problems.hint: Count the line ends and corners: each one is a carbon. Then check for branches.

explain.s-butane: Butane: four carbons in a zigzag row, no branches.
explain.s-isobutane: 2-Methylpropane: a three-carbon chain with a methyl on the middle carbon. Four carbons total, branched.

problems.prompt: Which formula could belong to an alkane?
problems.hint: Check each one against CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

explain.f-c6h14: Right! 2 × 6 + 2 = 14. C₆H₁₄ is hexane (or one of its isomers).
explain.f-c6h12: C₆H₁₂ is CₙH₂ₙ: two H's short. It needs a ring or a double bond, so it isn't an alkane.
explain.f-c6h10: C₆H₁₀ is four H's short of CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Not an alkane.
explain.f-c6h16: Impossible! Six carbons can hold at most 2 × 6 + 2 = 14 hydrogens. C₆H₁₆ would need a carbon with five bonds.

problems.prompt: Rank these from FEWEST carbons to MOST carbons.
problems.hint: Meth, eth, prop, but, pent: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

lesson.text: Alkanes are boring. That's the point. The interesting part of a molecule is its FUNCTIONAL GROUP: a group of atoms that reacts the same way in every molecule it's in. Big molecule, small molecule, doesn't matter.
Carbon–carbon multiple bonds: alkenes have C=C (-ene), alkynes have C≡C (-yne), and arenes have a six-carbon ring of alternating double and single bonds.
Carbon singly bonded to an electronegative atom: halides (C–X), alcohols (C–OH, -ol), ethers (C–O–C), amines (C–N, -amine), thiols (C–SH), sulfides (C–S–C), disulfides (C–S–S–C). Carbon ends up δ+.

Then the big family: the carbonyl, C=O. What ELSE is on the carbonyl carbon decides the name. At least one H: aldehyde (-al). Two carbons: ketone (-one). An –OH: carboxylic acid. An –OR: ester. A nitrogen: amide. A chlorine: acid chloride.
lesson.art: C=O + H · C · OH · OR · N · Cl

lesson.text: Worked example: acetone, CH₃COCH₃. The C=O carbon has two carbons on it. Two carbons on the carbonyl carbon means ketone. That's all I'm explaining.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: Find the C=O. What's attached to its carbon?

explain.fg-ketone: Right! The carbonyl carbon has two carbons attached, one on each side. That's a ketone (this one is butan-2-one).
explain.fg-aldehyde: An aldehyde needs an H on the carbonyl carbon. Here the C=O carbon has two carbons on it: a ketone.
explain.fg-ester: An ester needs an –O–C on the carbonyl carbon. This one has only carbons attached: a ketone.
explain.fg-acid: A carboxylic acid needs an –OH on the carbonyl carbon. There's no –OH here: it's a ketone.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: The C=O is at the END of the chain. What's on that carbon besides the chain?

explain.fg-aldehyde: Right! The C=O sits at the end of the chain, so its carbon carries an H. A carbonyl with an H on it is an aldehyde (this is propanal).
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone's carbonyl carbon has TWO carbons on it. This one is at the chain's end, with one carbon and one H: an aldehyde.
explain.fg-alcohol: An alcohol has C–OH. This oxygen is double-bonded, with no H: a carbonyl, here an aldehyde.
explain.fg-acid: A carboxylic acid needs an –OH on the carbonyl carbon too. This one only has an H: an aldehyde.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: What's on each side of the oxygen?

explain.fg-ether: Right! One oxygen with a carbon on each side: C–O–C. That's an ether (diethyl ether).
explain.fg-alcohol: An alcohol needs an O–H. This oxygen has carbons on both sides and no H: an ether.
explain.fg-ester: An ester needs a C=O next to the oxygen. There's no carbonyl here: just C–O–C, an ether.
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone needs a C=O. This oxygen is singly bonded to two carbons: an ether.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: There's a C=O AND another oxygen on the same carbon. What's on that second oxygen?

explain.fg-ester: Right! The carbonyl carbon also carries an –O–CH₃. A carbonyl plus an ether-like oxygen is an ester (methyl acetate).
explain.fg-acid: Close! A carboxylic acid has –OH on the carbonyl carbon. Here the second oxygen carries a CH₃, not an H: that's an ester.
explain.fg-ether: There IS a C–O–C, but its carbon is also a C=O. Carbonyl plus –O–C on the same carbon is an ester.
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone has only carbons on the carbonyl carbon. This one also has an oxygen: an ester.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: How is the nitrogen bonded? Is there a C=O anywhere?

explain.fg-amine: Right! A carbon singly bonded to nitrogen, with no C=O: an amine (ethylamine).
explain.fg-amide: An amide needs the nitrogen on a C=O carbon. There's no carbonyl here: it's an amine.
explain.fg-nitrile: A nitrile has C≡N, a triple bond. Here the C–N bond is single: an amine.
explain.fg-imine: An imine has C=N, a double bond. This C–N is single: an amine.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: The nitrogen and the C=O share a carbon.

explain.fg-amide: Right! The nitrogen sits on the carbonyl carbon. Carbonyl plus nitrogen on the same carbon is an amide (acetamide).
explain.fg-amine: There's a C–N, but that carbon is also C=O. Nitrogen on a carbonyl carbon makes an amide, which behaves very differently from an amine.
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone has two carbons on the carbonyl carbon. This one has a carbon and a nitrogen: an amide.
explain.fg-ester: An ester has an –O–C on the carbonyl carbon. This one has a nitrogen: an amide.

problems.prompt: What functional group does this molecule contain?
problems.hint: What's attached to the sulfur besides the chain?

explain.fg-thiol: Right! A carbon bonded to an –SH: a thiol (ethanethiol). It's the sulfur version of an alcohol.
explain.fg-sulfide: A sulfide has carbons on BOTH sides of the sulfur (C–S–C). This sulfur has one carbon and one H: a thiol.
explain.fg-alcohol: Alcohols have –OH. This is –SH, sulfur instead of oxygen: a thiol.
explain.fg-disulfide: A disulfide has two sulfurs bonded together (C–S–S–C). There's only one sulfur here: a thiol.

problems.prompt: This molecule (GABA, a brain chemical) has two functional groups. Name each one.
problems.hint: The N is at one end and the C=O at the other. Look at what's on each.

explain.fg-amine: Right! The –NH₂ is on a plain CH₂ carbon, with no C=O next to it: an amine.
explain.fg-acid: Right! The carbonyl carbon also has an –OH: a carboxylic acid.
explain.fg-amide: An amide needs the N on the carbonyl carbon itself. Here they're at opposite ends of the chain: an amine and a carboxylic acid.
explain.fg-ester: An ester needs –O–C on the carbonyl carbon. This one has –OH, with an H: a carboxylic acid.
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone has two carbons on the carbonyl carbon. This one has a carbon and an –OH: a carboxylic acid.

problems.prompt: Match each family to its name ending. (Table 3.1)
problems.hint: Methanol, acetone (propanone), propanal, ethene.

explain.end-ol: -ol is the alcohol ending: methanol, ethanol.
explain.end-one: -one is the ketone ending: propanone (acetone), butanone.
explain.end-al: -al is the aldehyde ending: propanal, ethanal.
explain.end-ene: -ene is the alkene ending: ethene, propene.
explain.end-oate: -oate is the ESTER ending (methyl ethanoate, for example). None of these four families uses it.

lesson.text: Alkanes are also called paraffins, from Latin for 'little affinity.' Accurate. They ignore most lab reagents. A lot like me.

They DO react with a few things. With oxygen, they burn: methane + 2 O₂ gives CO₂ + 2 H₂O and a lot of heat. With Cl₂ under UV light, the H's get swapped for Cl's one by one, giving a messy mixture: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, and CCl₄.
Alkanes are held together in the liquid only by DISPERSION forces, those weak, flickering temporary dipoles. Bigger molecules have more of them, so boiling points climb as chains get longer.

Branching LOWERS the boiling point. Pentane boils at 36.1 °C, 2-methylbutane at 27.85 °C, and 2,2-dimethylpropane at 9.5 °C. Same formula! Branched molecules are rounder, with less surface area, so less dispersion attraction.
Same story for octane, 125.7 °C, versus isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane), 99.3 °C. Rounder molecules touch less. Now leave me alone with my pigeons.

problems.prompt: These three C₅H₁₂ isomers boil at different temperatures. Rank them from HIGHEST to LOWEST boiling point.
problems.hint: More branches, rounder molecule, less surface area.

explain.s-pentane: Pentane, the straight chain: the most surface area and the strongest dispersion forces. bp 36.1 °C, the highest.
explain.s-isopentane: 2-Methylbutane: one branch. bp 27.85 °C, in the middle.
explain.s-neopentane: 2,2-Dimethylpropane: the roundest, almost a ball. bp 9.5 °C, the lowest.

problems.prompt: Why does branching LOWER an alkane's boiling point?
problems.hint: What force holds alkane molecules together in the liquid?

explain.bp-sphere: Right! Branched alkanes are more nearly spherical, with smaller surface areas, so they have weaker dispersion forces between molecules.
explain.bp-hbond: Alkanes can't hydrogen-bond: they have no O–H or N–H. Branching lowers bp because rounder molecules have less surface for dispersion forces.
explain.bp-lighter: Isomers have the SAME formula, so the same mass. The difference is shape: rounder means less surface area and weaker dispersion forces.
explain.bp-weakcc: Boiling doesn't break C–C bonds. It only pulls molecules apart, and rounder molecules have weaker dispersion forces between them.

problems.prompt: Octane boils at 125.7 °C. Isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) has the same formula, C₈H₁₈. What's its boiling point?
problems.hint: Isooctane has three branches.

explain.io-lower: Right! Isooctane is heavily branched and rounder, so its dispersion forces are weaker. It boils at 99.3 °C.
explain.io-higher: Branching LOWERS the boiling point. Isooctane is rounder than octane, so it boils lower, at 99.3 °C.
explain.io-same: Same formula, but different shapes and different properties. Isooctane's rounder shape gives weaker dispersion forces: bp 99.3 °C.

problems.prompt: Methane burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
problems.hint: Think of a gas stove.

explain.cb-co2: Right! CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, releasing a lot of heat. That's why natural gas is a fuel.
explain.cb-coh2: Complete combustion makes carbon dioxide and water: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.
explain.cb-meoh: Burning doesn't stop at methanol. Complete combustion goes all the way to CO₂ and H₂O.
explain.cb-none: Alkanes are unreactive toward most reagents, but they DO burn. CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O + heat.

problems.prompt: Methane and Cl₂ are mixed and hit with ultraviolet light. What forms?
problems.hint: There are four H's on methane, and nothing stops the reaction after the first one.

explain.cl-mix: Right! The hydrogens get replaced by chlorine one after another, so you get a mixture: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, and CCl₄. (More in Section 6.6.)
explain.cl-one: The reaction doesn't stop after one Cl. The other H's get substituted too, giving a mixture of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, and CCl₄.
explain.cl-alkene: One carbon can't make a C=C. Chlorine substitutes for H's, giving CH₃Cl through CCl₄.
explain.cb-none: In the dark, maybe. Under UV light, methane and Cl₂ react, giving a mixture of chloromethanes.

problems.prompt: Alkanes are also called 'paraffins' (Latin parum affinis). What does that say about them?
problems.hint: 'Parum' means little.

explain.pf-little: Right! 'Little affinity': alkanes are chemically inert to most lab reagents. They react only with oxygen, halogens, and a few others.
explain.pf-reactive: The opposite! Alkanes are among the LEAST reactive organic compounds. 'Paraffin' means 'little affinity.'
explain.pf-soluble: Alkanes are hydrophobic and barely dissolve in water. 'Paraffin' means 'little affinity': they're unreactive.
explain.pf-polar: C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar (EN 2.5 vs 2.1). 'Paraffin' means 'little affinity': they're unreactive.

problems.prompt: What attractive force holds liquid hexane molecules together?
problems.hint: Hexane is nonpolar and has no O–H or N–H.

explain.im-disp: Right! Only dispersion forces. They're weak individually but grow with molecular size, which is why bigger alkanes boil higher.
explain.im-dipole: Hexane has essentially no permanent dipole (C–H is nearly nonpolar). Only dispersion forces act.
explain.im-hbond: Hydrogen bonds need O–H or N–H. Hexane has only C–H: dispersion forces only.
explain.im-ionic: Hexane has no ions. Only weak dispersion forces hold the liquid together.

problems.prompt: Rank these straight-chain alkanes from LOWEST to HIGHEST boiling point. (Figure 3.5)
problems.hint: Bigger molecule, more dispersion force.
problems.why: Boiling points rise steadily with chain length: ethane < butane < hexane < decane.

explain.bp-ethane: Ethane, the smallest: weakest dispersion forces, lowest bp (a gas well below room temperature).
explain.bp-butane: Butane: 4 carbons. Still a gas at room temperature, but it boils higher than ethane.
explain.bp-hexane: Hexane: 6 carbons. A liquid at room temperature.
explain.bp-decane: Decane: 10 carbons. The largest, with the most dispersion force: the highest bp.

lesson.text: Isomers: same formula, different arrangement. If the CONNECTIONS differ, they're constitutional isomers. Different compounds. Different properties. Don't mix them up or I'll sulk. More than usual.
The number of alkane isomers explodes. C₄H₁₀: 2. C₅H₁₂: 3. C₆H₁₄: 5. C₇H₁₆: 9. C₁₀H₂₂: 75. C₂₀H₄₂: over 366,000. (Table 3.2)

Isomers don't have to be alkanes. They can differ in skeleton (butane vs. isobutane), functional group (ethanol vs. dimethyl ether, both C₂H₆O), or where a group sits (propylamine vs. isopropylamine).

Pull an H off an alkane and you get an ALKYL GROUP: -ane becomes -yl. Methyl –CH₃, ethyl –CH₂CH₃, propyl, butyl. Pull the H from an inner carbon and you get branched ones: isopropyl –CH(CH₃)₂, sec-butyl, isobutyl, tert-butyl –C(CH₃)₃.

Carbons get ranks by how many OTHER carbons they're bonded to: one is primary (1°), two is secondary (2°), three is tertiary (3°), four is quaternary (4°). Hydrogens take the rank of their carbon. There's no quaternary hydrogen. Think about why.
Worked example: isobutane, (CH₃)₃CH. The middle carbon touches three carbons, so it's tertiary, and its lone H is a tertiary H. The three CH₃ carbons are primary, with 9 primary H's. Done. Shoo.

problems.prompt: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C₆H₁₄? (Problem 3-4, Table 3.2)
problems.hint: Hexane, two methylpentanes, and two dimethylbutanes.

explain.n4: One short. Don't forget there are TWO dimethylbutanes (2,2- and 2,3-). The total is 5.
explain.n6: One too many. Watch for duplicates: '4-methylpentane' is just 2-methylpentane numbered from the wrong end. The total is 5.
explain.n9: Nine is the count for C₇H₁₆. C₆H₁₄ has 5.

problems.prompt: How many ALCOHOLS have the formula C₃H₈O? (Problem 3-6a)
problems.hint: Put the –OH on an end carbon, then on the middle carbon.

explain.n2: Right! Two: 1-propanol (–OH on an end carbon) and 2-propanol (–OH on the middle carbon).
explain.n1: The –OH can go on an end carbon OR the middle carbon. That's 2: 1-propanol and 2-propanol.
explain.n3: Both end carbons are the same position, so they count once. Only 2: 1-propanol and 2-propanol. (Methyl ethyl ether is also C₃H₈O, but it's an ether.)
explain.n4: Too many. Only two alcohols: 1-propanol and 2-propanol.

problems.prompt: How many BROMOALKANES have the formula C₄H₉Br? (Problem 3-6b)
problems.hint: Try both C₄ skeletons (straight and branched), and every unique spot for Br on each.

explain.n4: Right! Four: 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane on the straight chain, and 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane on the branched one.
explain.n2: That's only the straight chain. The branched C₄ skeleton gives two more, so 4 in all.
explain.n3: One short. Each skeleton has TWO unique positions for Br, so 4 in all.
explain.n5: One too many. Watch for duplicates numbered from opposite ends. There are 4.

problems.prompt: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃) are both C₂H₆O. What are they?
problems.hint: Is the O connected the same way in both?

explain.iso-const: Right! Same formula, different connections: C–C–O–H vs C–O–C. Constitutional isomers with DIFFERENT functional groups (an alcohol and an ether).
explain.iso-same: Ethanol has C–C–O and dimethyl ether has C–O–C. No redrawing changes that. Different compounds: constitutional isomers.
explain.iso-conf: No bond rotation turns C–C–O into C–O–C. The connections differ, so they're constitutional isomers.
explain.iso-diff: Count again: both are C₂H₆O. Same formula, different connections: constitutional isomers.

problems.prompt: In 2,2-dimethylbutane, what kind of carbon is C2 (the one carrying both methyls)?
problems.hint: Count the carbons bonded to C2: C1, C3, and the two methyls.

explain.c-quaternary: Right! C2 is bonded to C1, C3, and two methyls: four other carbons. That's quaternary (4°), and it has no hydrogens left.
explain.c-tertiary: Tertiary means three carbon neighbors. C2 has four (C1, C3, and two methyls): quaternary.
explain.c-secondary: Secondary means two carbon neighbors, like a CH₂ in a chain. C2 has four: quaternary.
explain.c-primary: Primary means one carbon neighbor, like a CH₃ end. C2 has four: quaternary.

problems.prompt: Match each alkyl group to its name. (Figure 3.4)
problems.hint: Look at the attachment carbon (written first). How many carbons are bonded to it?

explain.ag-iso: Isopropyl, –CH(CH₃)₂: three carbons, attached through the MIDDLE one.
explain.ag-tert: tert-Butyl, –C(CH₃)₃: four carbons, attached through a tertiary carbon that carries three methyls.
explain.ag-isobu: Isobutyl, –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂: four carbons, attached through an end CH₂, with the branch one carbon away.
explain.ag-sec: sec-Butyl, –CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃: four carbons in a row, attached through a secondary (inner) carbon.

problems.prompt: There are primary, secondary, and tertiary hydrogens, but no QUATERNARY hydrogens. Why not?
problems.hint: How many bonds does a quaternary carbon have left over?

explain.qh-room: Right! A quaternary carbon uses all four bonds on other carbons. There's no bond left for a hydrogen.
explain.qh-acidic: It's not about acidity. A quaternary carbon has four carbon neighbors, so it has no room for an H at all.
explain.qh-rare: They don't exist at all. A quaternary carbon's four bonds all go to carbons.
explain.qh-methyl: Methyl H's are PRIMARY (a CH₃ has one carbon neighbor). Quaternary carbons have no H's at all.

problems.prompt: 'Citric acid is a TERTIARY alcohol.' What does that tell you?
problems.hint: 1°, 2°, 3° count something on the carbon holding the group.

explain.ta-3c: Right! A tertiary alcohol has its –OH on a carbon that is itself bonded to three other carbons.
explain.ta-3oh: 'Tertiary' isn't a count of –OH groups. It means the –OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons.
explain.ta-3h: A carbon with an –OH and three H's would be methanol's carbon, with zero carbon neighbors. Tertiary means three CARBON neighbors.
explain.ta-c3: It's not a position number. Tertiary means the –OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons.

problems.prompt: How many TERTIARY hydrogens does 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, have?
problems.hint: Find the tertiary carbon first. How many H's does it hold?

explain.n1: Right! The central carbon is bonded to three carbons (tertiary) and holds just ONE hydrogen. The other 9 H's are on primary CH₃ carbons.
explain.n3: Three is the number of carbons on the central carbon. That carbon holds only one H, so there's 1 tertiary H.
explain.n9: Those 9 are on the three CH₃ groups, which are PRIMARY carbons. The one tertiary H is on the central carbon.
explain.n0: The central carbon is tertiary (three carbon neighbors), and it still has room for one H. So there's 1.

lesson.text: Naming. Finally, rules. I like rules. Rules don't ask me to smile. An IUPAC name has a parent (the main chain), prefixes (substituents), and locants (numbers that say where).
Step 1: find the LONGEST continuous chain, even if you have to turn corners. That's the parent. If two chains tie, pick the one with MORE branch points.
Step 2: number from the end NEARER the first branch. If the first branches tie, go to the second branch. Step 3: give every substituent a number. Two on the same carbon? Both get that number.

Step 4: write it as one word. Commas between numbers, hyphens between numbers and words. List different substituents ALPHABETICALLY. Use di-, tri-, tetra- for repeats, but IGNORE those for alphabetizing.
Common names are allowed for a few groups: isopropyl, isobutyl, sec-butyl, tert-butyl. For alphabetizing, 'iso' counts (isopropyl goes under i), but sec- and tert- don't (tert-butyl goes under b).

Worked example: 2,3-dimethylpentane. The longest chain is 5 (pentane). Numbering from the left puts methyls on C2 and C3, which beats C3 and C4 from the right. Two methyls make 'dimethyl.' Now you do it.

problems.prompt: Give the IUPAC name. (Problem 3-11b)
problems.hint: Longest chain first, then number from the end closer to a branch.

explain.na-23dmp: Right! The longest chain is 5 carbons (pentane). Numbering from the end nearer the branches puts methyls on C2 and C3.
explain.na-34dmp: Right chain, wrong end. Number from the end NEARER the first branch: 2,3 beats 3,4.
explain.na-2e3mb: That chain is only 4 long. Going through the 'ethyl' gives a 5-carbon chain, so the parent is pentane: 2,3-dimethylpentane.
explain.na-heptane: It has 7 carbons (C₇H₁₆), but heptane is the STRAIGHT 7-chain. This one branches: 2,3-dimethylpentane.

problems.prompt: Give the IUPAC name. (Problem 3-11c)
problems.hint: Two identical substituents get one multiplier prefix.

explain.na-24dmp: Right! A 5-carbon chain with methyls on C2 and C4. Two methyls: 2,4-dimethylpentane.
explain.na-13dmp: A methyl on C1 means you didn't use the longest chain. That 'methyl' is really part of the chain. The longest chain is 5 with methyls on 2 and 4.
explain.na-2m4mp: Identical substituents get combined with a multiplier: 2,4-DImethylpentane, not 2-methyl-4-methyl.
explain.nm-3mp: 3-Methylpentane has only 6 carbons. This molecule has 7: 2,4-dimethylpentane.

problems.prompt: Give the IUPAC name. (Problem 3-11d)
problems.hint: Both ends hit a branch at C2. Then compare the next number.

explain.na-225tmh: Right! The longest chain is 6 (hexane). Either end gives a first branch at C2, so compare the next: 2,2,5 beats 2,5,5.
explain.na-255tmh: Both ends reach a branch at C2, so look at the next branch: 2,2,5 is lower than 2,5,5 at the first difference.
explain.na-225tmhep: Count the main chain again: 6 carbons, so hexane. The 9 carbons include 3 methyls.
explain.na-24dmp: This has 9 carbons, not 7. Hexane chain with three methyls: 2,2,5-trimethylhexane.

problems.prompt: Give the IUPAC name.
problems.hint: Two different 6-carbon chains tie. Pick the one with more branch points. Then alphabetize.

explain.na-3e2mh: Right! Six-carbon chain with two branch points: a methyl on C2 and an ethyl on C3. Alphabetical: ethyl before methyl.
explain.na-2m3eh: Right numbers, wrong order. Substituents are listed alphabetically: Ethyl comes before Methyl. 3-Ethyl-2-methylhexane.
explain.na-4e5mh: You numbered from the wrong end. The first branch should get the LOWEST number: C2, not C5.
explain.na-3iph: That 6-chain has only ONE branch point. A tying 6-chain with TWO branch points wins (Rule 1b): 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane.

problems.prompt: Which structure is 3-isopropyl-2-methylhexane? (Worked Example 3.3)
problems.hint: Draw hexane, put a methyl on C2 and an isopropyl on C3, right next to it.

explain.s-3ip2mh: Right! A hexane chain with a methyl on C2 and an isopropyl, –CH(CH₃)₂, on the neighboring C3.
explain.s-4iph: This one is 4-isopropylheptane: the isopropyl sits in the middle of a 7-carbon chain, and there's no 2-methyl.
explain.s-ipfar: This has the isopropyl group farther down the chain, not on C3 right next to the methyl-bearing C2.
explain.s-2mh: This is 2-methylhexane, with no isopropyl group at all.

problems.prompt: A name contains these four prefixes. Put them in the order they're CITED (alphabetical).
problems.hint: Ignore 'tert-' and 'di-'. Keep 'iso'.
problems.why: Alphabetize on butyl (b), ethyl (e), isopropyl (i), methyl (m). tert- and di- are ignored; iso is part of the name.

explain.ab-tbu: tert-Butyl alphabetizes under B (tert- is ignored), so it comes FIRST.
explain.ab-ipr: Isopropyl alphabetizes under I, because the unhyphenated 'iso' counts. Third.
explain.ab-dime: Dimethyl alphabetizes under M, because the multiplier 'di' is ignored. Last.

problems.prompt: Someone named a compound '4-methylpentane.' That breaks a numbering rule. What's the correct name?
problems.hint: Renumber from the other end of the chain.

explain.nm-2mp: Right! Number from the end nearer the branch: a methyl on C4 counted one way is on C2 counted the other way. 2-Methylpentane.
explain.nm-4mp: That's the broken name. Number from the end nearer the branch: 2-methylpentane.
explain.nm-3mp: 3-Methylpentane is a DIFFERENT compound (the methyl is in the exact middle). C4 from one end is C2 from the other: 2-methylpentane.
explain.nm-2mb: Renumbering doesn't change the chain length. It's still pentane: 2-methylpentane.

lesson.text: Ah. MY chapter. Single bonds are cylindrically symmetrical, so they can ROTATE. Each different arrangement from rotation is a CONFORMATION. Molecules in different conformations are conformers.

A Newman projection looks straight down a C–C bond, end-on. Like I do. All day. Every day. The front carbon is a dot where its three bonds meet in the CENTER. The back carbon is a circle, and its bonds stick out from the circle's EDGE.
lesson.art: front: to center · back: from the edge

lesson.text: Rotation isn't perfectly free. In ethane, STAGGERED (bonds 60° apart, as far as possible) is the most stable. ECLIPSED (bonds lined up) is the least stable, 12 kJ/mol higher. At any instant about 99% of ethane molecules are roughly staggered.
That extra 12 kJ/mol is TORSIONAL STRAIN. There are three H↔H eclipsing interactions, so each one costs about 4.0 kJ/mol (1.0 kcal/mol). Mind the units.
Conformers interconvert far too fast to separate. Spin the back carbon: staggered, eclipsed, staggered, eclipsed, every 60°. Energy minimum, maximum, minimum. Like my mood.

problems.prompt: How much higher in energy is ethane's eclipsed conformation than its staggered one?
problems.hint: Three H↔H eclipsing interactions in total.

explain.e-12: Right! 12 kJ/mol (2.9 kcal/mol): three H↔H eclipsing interactions at about 4.0 kJ/mol each.
explain.e-4: 4.0 kJ/mol is ONE H↔H interaction. Eclipsed ethane has three, for a total of 12 kJ/mol.
explain.e-38: 3.8 kJ/mol is butane's gauche (steric) strain. Ethane's eclipsing barrier is 12 kJ/mol.
explain.e-19: 19 kJ/mol is butane's fully eclipsed conformation. Ethane's barrier is 12 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: Ethane's 12 kJ/mol barrier comes from three equal H↔H eclipsing interactions. How much does EACH one cost?
problems.hint: Divide, and watch the units.

explain.e-4: Right! 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0 kJ/mol per H↔H eclipsing interaction (which is 1.0 kcal/mol).
explain.e-12: 12 kJ/mol is the TOTAL for all three. Each one is 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0 kJ/mol.
explain.e-1kj: Unit trap! It's 1.0 kcal/mol, which is 4.0 kJ/mol. Not 1.0 kJ/mol.
explain.e-6: 6.0 kJ/mol is an H↔CH₃ eclipsing interaction (from propane). H↔H is 4.0 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: What is the extra energy of ethane's eclipsed conformation called?
problems.hint: It's about bonds on neighboring carbons lining up, not atoms bumping into each other.

explain.st-torsional: Right! Torsional strain: the cost of eclipsed bonds on neighboring carbons. In ethane, mostly from C–H bonding/antibonding orbital interactions favoring staggered.
explain.st-steric: Steric strain is atoms crammed closer than their size allows, like the methyls in gauche butane. Ethane's tiny H's give torsional strain.
explain.st-angle: Angle strain comes from squeezed bond angles, as in small rings (next floor). Ethane's angles are normal: this is torsional strain.
explain.st-resonance: Resonance isn't involved. Ethane's eclipsed form is higher in energy because of torsional strain.

problems.prompt: In a Newman projection, how are the bonds to the BACK carbon drawn?
problems.hint: The back carbon is hidden behind a circle.

explain.nw-edge: Right! The back carbon is the circle, so its bonds start at the circle's edge. The front carbon's bonds meet at the center.
explain.nw-center: Bonds meeting at the center belong to the FRONT carbon. The back carbon's bonds come out from the circle's edge.
explain.nw-wedge: Wedges are for regular 3-D drawings. In a Newman projection, back-carbon bonds come off the circle's edge.
explain.nw-dash: Dashes are for regular 3-D drawings. In a Newman projection, back-carbon bonds come off the circle's edge.

problems.prompt: Why can't you fill one bottle with staggered ethane and another with eclipsed ethane?
problems.hint: How high is the barrier compared to room-temperature energy?

explain.cf-fast: Right! The barrier is only 12 kJ/mol, so conformers interconvert far too rapidly to isolate. (Unlike constitutional isomers, which you can bottle separately.)
explain.cf-explode: Eclipsed ethane is only 12 kJ/mol higher. It just rotates back. The conformers interconvert too quickly to separate.
explain.cf-formula: Conformers have the same formula AND the same connections. They only differ by rotation, which happens too fast to separate them.
explain.cf-norot: C–C single bonds rotate easily, which is exactly why you can't separate conformers. They interconvert constantly.

problems.prompt: At any given instant, roughly what fraction of ethane molecules are in an approximately staggered conformation?
problems.hint: Staggered is lower in energy by 12 kJ/mol, but rotation never stops.

explain.pc-99: Right! About 99% are near staggered, and only about 1% are near eclipsed at any instant.
explain.pc-50: If both were equally stable, maybe. Staggered is 12 kJ/mol lower, so about 99% are near staggered.
explain.pc-1: Backwards: about 1% are near ECLIPSED. About 99% are near staggered.
explain.pc-100: Not quite all. Rotation never stops, so about 1% are passing through eclipsed at any instant. About 99% are staggered.

problems.prompt: Start ethane in a staggered conformation (0°). Rotate the back carbon in 60° steps. What conformation do you reach at each step?
problems.hint: Staggered and eclipsed alternate every 60°.
problems.why: Staggered (0°) → eclipsed (60°) → staggered (120°) → eclipsed (180°): they alternate every 60°.

explain.cn-ecl: Eclipsed: 60° from any staggered conformation, the front and back C–H bonds line up.
explain.cn-stag: Staggered: another 60° turns eclipsed back into staggered.
explain.cn-gauche: 'Gauche' describes two LARGE groups 60° apart, as in butane. Ethane has only H's, so its staggered forms are all identical.

lesson.text: Bigger alkanes, bigger problems. Propane's barrier is 14 kJ/mol. Its eclipsed form has two H↔H interactions (4.0 each) and one H↔CH₃. So H↔CH₃ costs 14 − 8 = 6.0 kJ/mol.
Now butane, looking down C2–C3. ANTI: the methyls are 180° apart. The most stable. Rotate 60°: eclipsed, with two CH₃↔H plus one H↔H, 2(6.0) + 4.0 = 16 kJ/mol.
Another 60°: GAUCHE. Staggered, but the methyls are 60° apart, close enough to bump. That's STERIC STRAIN: atoms forced closer than their size allows. Gauche is 3.8 kJ/mol above anti.
Another 60°: methyls fully eclipsed. Torsional AND steric strain: 19 kJ/mol. Subtract the two H↔H (8.0), and CH₃↔CH₃ eclipsing costs 11 kJ/mol. Then the cycle mirrors back. (Table 3.5)

Rule of thumb: the most stable conformation of any alkane is staggered, with the big groups anti. And 'more stable' doesn't mean stuck. Everything keeps interconverting; the stable one is just the most common at any moment.
Worked example: 1-chloropropane, sighting down C1–C2. Most stable: staggered with Cl anti to CH₃. Least stable: eclipsed with Cl lined up on CH₃. Now go. I've talked more today than in a century.

problems.prompt: What is propane's barrier to rotation around a C–C bond?
problems.hint: Slightly higher than ethane's, because one H is now a CH₃.

explain.e-14: Right! 14 kJ/mol (3.4 kcal/mol): two H↔H (4.0 each) plus one H↔CH₃ (6.0).
explain.e-12: 12 kJ/mol is ethane's. Propane's is a bit higher, 14 kJ/mol, because one eclipsing partner is a CH₃.
explain.e-16: 16 kJ/mol is butane's CH₃↔H eclipsed form. Propane's barrier is 14 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: Propane's barrier is 14 kJ/mol. Its eclipsed form has two H↔H interactions (4.0 kJ/mol each) and one H↔CH₃. What does the H↔CH₃ interaction cost?
problems.hint: Subtract what you already know from the total.

explain.e-6: Right! 14 − 2(4.0) = 6.0 kJ/mol (1.4 kcal/mol). Mostly torsional strain.
explain.e-10: You subtracted only ONE H↔H. There are two: 14 − 8.0 = 6.0 kJ/mol.
explain.e-4: 4.0 kJ/mol is H↔H. The bulkier H↔CH₃ costs more: 14 − 8.0 = 6.0 kJ/mol.
explain.e-14: 14 kJ/mol is the total for all three interactions. H↔CH₃ alone is 14 − 8.0 = 6.0 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: Rank butane's conformations (around C2–C3) from MOST stable to LEAST stable. (Figure 3.10)
problems.hint: Staggered beats eclipsed. Then: how close are the methyls?
problems.why: Anti 0 < gauche 3.8 < eclipsed CH₃↔H 16 < eclipsed CH₃↔CH₃ 19 kJ/mol.

explain.cn-anti: Anti (180°): staggered, methyls as far apart as possible. The energy minimum.
explain.cn-gauche: Gauche (60°): staggered, but the methyls bump. 3.8 kJ/mol of steric strain.
explain.cn-ecl-mm: Eclipsed, CH₃↔CH₃ (0°): torsional plus steric strain, 19 kJ/mol. The energy maximum.

problems.prompt: Gauche butane has NO eclipsing interactions, yet it's 3.8 kJ/mol above anti. What kind of strain is that?
problems.hint: The methyls aren't eclipsed. They're just too close.

explain.st-steric: Right! Steric strain: the methyl groups' hydrogens are forced closer than their atomic radii allow.
explain.st-torsional: Torsional strain comes from ECLIPSED bonds. Gauche is staggered. Its 3.8 kJ/mol is steric strain from the crowded methyls.
explain.st-angle: Butane's bond angles are normal. Gauche strain comes from methyls bumping: steric strain.
explain.st-hbond: C–H's don't hydrogen-bond, and H-bonds would LOWER the energy anyway. This is steric strain.

problems.prompt: Sight down the C2–C1 bond of 2-methylpropane. Its eclipsed conformation has two H↔CH₃ interactions and one H↔H. What's the barrier? (Problem 3-16)
problems.hint: H↔CH₃ is 6.0 kJ/mol and H↔H is 4.0 kJ/mol.

explain.e-14: That's propane, with only ONE H↔CH₃. 2-Methylpropane has two: 2(6.0) + 4.0 = 16 kJ/mol.
explain.e-12: That's ethane, with three H↔H. Here two of them are H↔CH₃: 2(6.0) + 4.0 = 16 kJ/mol.
explain.e-18: That would be three H↔CH₃. Only two methyls are on C2 here: 2(6.0) + 4.0 = 16 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: Butane's fully eclipsed conformation (methyls lined up) costs 19 kJ/mol total. It also has two H↔H eclipses (4.0 each). What does CH₃↔CH₃ eclipsing cost?
problems.hint: Total minus the two H↔H.

explain.e-11: Right! 19 − 2(4.0) = 11 kJ/mol (2.6 kcal/mol): torsional plus steric strain.
explain.e-19: 19 kJ/mol is the whole conformation. Subtract the two H↔H: 19 − 8.0 = 11 kJ/mol.
explain.e-15: You subtracted only one H↔H. There are two: 19 − 8.0 = 11 kJ/mol.
explain.e-38: 3.8 kJ/mol is the GAUCHE interaction (staggered). Eclipsed CH₃↔CH₃ is 19 − 8.0 = 11 kJ/mol.

problems.prompt: Sight down the C1–C2 bond of 1-chloropropane, ClCH₂–CH₂CH₃. Which conformation is MOST stable? (Worked Example 3.4)
problems.hint: Staggered first, then keep the two big groups as far apart as possible.

explain.cp-anti: Right! Staggered, with the two largest groups (Cl and CH₃) anti, 180° apart.
explain.cp-gauche: Staggered is good, but Cl and CH₃ 60° apart crowd each other. Anti is better.
explain.cp-eclmm: That's the LEAST stable: eclipsed, with the two biggest groups lined up.
explain.cp-eclh: Any eclipsed conformation has torsional strain. Staggered with Cl anti to CH₃ is the most stable.

problems.prompt: Sight down C2–C3 of 2,3-dimethylbutane. Each carbon has two CH₃'s and one H. In the MOST stable conformation, how many CH₃↔CH₃ gauche interactions are there? (Problem 3-17)
problems.hint: Try putting the two H's anti to each other. Then check each front methyl against each back methyl.

explain.n2: Right! With the two H's anti, each front methyl is gauche to one back methyl and anti to the other. Two gauche interactions, 2 × 3.8 = 7.6 kJ/mol. The other staggered option has three.
explain.n0: With four methyls on two neighboring carbons, you can't put every pair anti. The best arrangement (H's anti) still has 2 gauche pairs.
explain.n1: Count both front methyls. With the H's anti, EACH front methyl is gauche to one back methyl: 2 in total.
explain.n3: That's the other staggered conformation (H's gauche). Putting the H's anti cuts it to 2, which is the most stable.

problems.prompt: 'Anti butane is more stable than gauche butane.' What does that actually mean?
problems.hint: Rotation at room temperature is very fast.

explain.eq-more: Right! All conformers are in rapid equilibrium. At any instant, a larger percentage of molecules happens to be anti.
explain.eq-locked: Nothing is locked. Rotation is so fast that every molecule keeps passing through all the conformations. Anti is just the most common.
explain.eq-never: Gauche absolutely forms: it's only 3.8 kJ/mol higher. It's just less common than anti at any instant.
explain.eq-formula: Anti and gauche are the SAME compound, just rotated. They're conformers, not different compounds.

intro.speaker: boss
intro.text: A gargoyle? THIS is your teacher now? A lump of stone that can only look at things end-on? How fitting. Stone memorizes. Stone never asks why.

intro.speaker: npc
intro.text: Hmph. I may be stone, Mordant, but I know WHY gauche costs 3.8 and anti costs nothing. You just carved the numbers into the wall.

intro.speaker: boss
intro.text: Then let's twist some chains, child. I'll scramble every name and eclipse every bond!

wrong: Longest chain? Who has time to count?
You numbered from the wrong end. Again.
right: Hmph. The gargoyle's grumbling sank in.
Fine. But my chains have more branches than that.

defeat.speaker: boss
defeat.text: Impossible! You found the longest chain... around a CORNER!

defeat.speaker: npc
defeat.text: That's what happens when you understand the rules instead of memorizing names. Not bad, climber. ...Don't tell anyone I said that.

defeat.speaker: boss
defeat.text: Enjoy your straight lines. Upstairs, the chains close into RINGS, and rings don't rotate so easily...

story.speaker: narrator
story.text: Mordant's tangled chains unravel into neat, staggered zigzags. He vanishes up the stairwell in a puff of purple smoke.

story.speaker: npc
story.text: Take this. A chip of my own stone skin. Use it on a hard problem, and your mistakes there won't cost you a thing. You'll still have to read why you were wrong, though. I insist.

story.speaker: narrator
story.text: As you climb toward Floor 4, you hear fussy muttering from above: someone rearranging furniture and complaining about 'axial clutter.'

legendary.name: Gargoyle's Stone Skin
legendary.desc: For the rest of the current problem, wrong cards cost no hearts. They still flip and explain why. Won from Floor 3's boss.

problems.prompt: Give the IUPAC name.
problems.hint: Count the longest chain, then pick the end that reaches a branch first.

explain.na-224tmh: Right! The longest chain is 6 (hexane). Numbering from the end with two methyls on one carbon gives 2,2,4. The other end gives 3,5,5.
explain.na-355tmh: Wrong end. From the other end, the first branch is at C2, not C3: 2,2,4-trimethylhexane.
explain.na-244tmh: That would put two methyls on C4. Here the carbon with two methyls is C2 (counted from the nearer end), and the single methyl is on C4.
explain.na-224tmp: Count the chain again: the longest chain has 6 carbons, so hexane. (2,2,4-Trimethylpentane is isooctane, with 8 carbons.)

problems.prompt: Arecoline (Problem 3-3) contains an amine and a C=C. What's its oxygen-containing functional group?
problems.hint: Find the C=O. Its carbon has another oxygen on it. What's on THAT oxygen?

explain.fg-ester: Right! The carbonyl carbon also carries –O–CH₃. Carbonyl plus –OR is an ester (a methyl ester).
explain.fg-acid: A carboxylic acid needs –OH on the carbonyl carbon. Here the second oxygen carries a CH₃: an ester.
explain.fg-ether: The –O–CH₃ is attached to a C=O carbon, which makes the whole thing an ester, not an ether.
explain.fg-ketone: A ketone has two CARBONS on its carbonyl carbon. This one has a carbon and an oxygen: an ester.

problems.prompt: Rank from HIGHEST to LOWEST boiling point.
problems.hint: Size matters most. Then, within the same size, branching lowers bp.
problems.why: Octane 125.7 °C > isooctane 99.3 °C > pentane 36.1 °C > neopentane 9.5 °C. The C₈'s beat the C₅'s, and branching lowers each pair.

explain.bb-octane: Octane: 8 carbons in a row. Biggest and least branched: 125.7 °C.
explain.bb-isooctane: Isooctane: also 8 carbons, but branched, so lower: 99.3 °C. Still far above the C₅'s.
explain.bb-neopentane: Neopentane: 5 carbons balled up. The lowest: 9.5 °C.

problems.prompt: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C₅H₁₂?
problems.hint: Straight, one branch, two branches on the same carbon.

explain.n2: Two is the count for C₄H₁₀. C₅H₁₂ has 3.
explain.n4: One too many. Watch for duplicates numbered from opposite ends: there are only 3.
explain.n5: Five is the count for C₆H₁₄. C₅H₁₂ has 3.

problems.prompt: On a graph of butane's energy vs. rotation around C2–C3, where is the lowest point?
problems.hint: Staggered, with the methyls as far apart as possible.

explain.cn-anti: Right! Anti, at 180°: staggered with the methyls opposite each other. Zero strain on this graph.
explain.cn-gauche: Gauche IS a minimum, but a local one, 3.8 kJ/mol up. Anti is the lowest point.
explain.cn-ecl-mm: That's the HIGHEST point (19 kJ/mol), with the methyls eclipsed.
explain.cn-ecl-mh: That's a maximum (16 kJ/mol). The lowest point is anti.

problems.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

slots.label: Strain from atoms crammed too close
Differ only by rotation around single bonds

problems.hint: Two are strains, two are isomer relationships.

explain.t-torsional: Torsional strain: the cost of eclipsing bonds on neighboring carbons (ethane's 12 kJ/mol).
explain.t-steric: Steric strain: atoms forced closer than their radii allow (gauche butane's 3.8 kJ/mol).
explain.t-const: Constitutional isomers: same formula, different connections, like butane and isobutane.
explain.t-conformers: Conformers: the same molecule in different rotational arrangements, like anti and gauche butane.

problems.prompt: 4-Isopropylheptane can also be given a fully systematic name. Which one?
problems.hint: Name the substituent like its own compound, numbering from where it attaches.

explain.ip-1me: Right! Isopropyl is a 2-carbon ethyl group with a methyl on its C1 (the attachment carbon): 1-methylethyl. So: 4-(1-methylethyl)heptane.
explain.ip-1mp: 1-Methylpropyl is sec-butyl, with four carbons. Isopropyl has three: 1-methylethyl.
explain.ip-prop: Propyl is a straight 3-carbon group attached at its end. Isopropyl attaches at the MIDDLE carbon: 1-methylethyl.
explain.ip-2m3p: That chain is only 6 long. The longest chain here is 7 (heptane), so the parent must be heptane.
